declarations.documentation:
Signal a typed error the caller may recover from. The payload is a domain-specific error `data`
(e.g. `json.parse_error`); a handler at that payload type catches it — `use handler { request
throw(error: my_error) -> never { break fallback } }` — and an unhandled throw fails the run with
the payload. `-> never` means a throw cannot be resumed: a handler recovers by `break`ing out of
the handle (or rethrows).
declarations.name: throw

parameters.documentation: The error payload; a handler naming this payload type catches it.
parameters.label: error

declarations.signature: request throw[T](error: T) -> never

declarations.documentation:
Run @task@ and turn EVERY error it throws into a value with @recover@ — the expression form of the
handler-and-break composition apps kept respelling. The catch is TOTAL: @F@ is the union of the
task's throws (the `lacks` on @E@ is what makes that the whole story), so nothing flies past. To let
SOME errors keep flying, match inside @recover@ is no use (it cannot rethrow into @E@) — write the
handler yourself and rethrow the match residual (`case rest -> throw(error = rest)`).
declarations.name: catch

parameters.documentation: The task whose throws are caught; every other effect passes through.
parameters.label: task

parameters.documentation: Turns a thrown error into the result value.
parameters.label: recover

declarations.signature: agent catch[T, F, effect E](task: agent(value: null) -> T with {...E, throw[F]}, recover: agent(error: F) -> T with E) -> T with E

declarations.documentation:
Run @task@ and turn ANY error — whatever its type, declared or not — into a value with @recover@:
the supervisor shape. Unlike `catch` (whose @F@ names the union and whose @E@ must lack `throw`),
here @E@ stays fully generic: the handler at `unknown` covers every instantiation a generic row
could carry, and the SUBTRACTION FORM in the result row is the signature-level proof that nothing
thrown escapes. @recover@ receives the payload as `unknown` — match on it (`case my_error(...)`)
to tell anticipated errors apart, and rethrowing is not an option here (the row already lacks
`throw`); use `catch` or a hand-written handler with a residual rethrow when some errors should
keep flying.
declarations.name: catch_all

parameters.documentation: The task whose throws are all caught; every other effect passes through.
parameters.label: task

parameters.documentation: Turns any thrown error into the result value.
parameters.label: recover

declarations.signature: agent catch_all[T, effect E](task: agent(value: null) -> T with E, recover: agent(error: unknown) -> T with {...E}) -> T with {...E}

parameters.label: key

key.description: The secret entry's key in the project's env store.

declarations.signature: data env(key: string)

declarations.documentation:
A named credential in the runtime's credential store — `resolve` reads it with `oauth.token` at
each use, so a refreshed token is always the current one. An unusable credential throws
`oauth.server_error` (and may park the run on an authorization escalation, like any `oauth.token`).
declarations.name: oauth

parameters.documentation: The credential's name in the runtime's credential store.
parameters.label: name

name.description: The credential's name in the runtime's credential store.

declarations.signature: data oauth(name: string)

declarations.name: source
declarations.signature: type source = env | oauth

declarations.documentation:
Resolve a credential source to its CURRENT value, as a private string. Called by a package's
provider once per `credential` request, never cached — freshness is the point.
declarations.name: resolve
declarations.signature: agent resolve(source: source) -> string of private with io | prelude.throw[missing_secret | server_error]

declarations.documentation:
The SHA-256 digest of @text@'s UTF-8 bytes, as 64 lowercase hex characters. Deterministic and pure,
so a replay recomputes the same digest. Typical uses: a content dedupe key, or a stable tag for an
external identifier — but note that a plain digest of an ENUMERABLE input (a numeric user id, an
email) is reversible by dictionary: anyone can hash every candidate and match. For a tag that must
not be reversible, use `hmac_sha256` with a secret key. Takes PUBLIC text only — hashing a secret
would raise a declassification question (is the digest of a secret still secret?) that this plain
digest deliberately leaves unanswered; `hmac_sha256` answers it for the keyed form.
declarations.name: sha256

parameters.documentation: The text to digest, hashed as its UTF-8 bytes.
parameters.label: text

text.description: The text to digest, hashed as its UTF-8 bytes.

declarations.signature: primitive agent sha256(text: string) -> string

declarations.documentation:
The HMAC-SHA-256 tag of @text@ under the secret @key@, as 64 lowercase hex characters — the
IRREVERSIBLE tag `sha256` cannot give over an enumerable input: without the key a dictionary attack
is impossible, so hashing a user id with a secret key yields a pseudonym that is stable for one key
and opaque to everyone without it (a chat bot's abuse-attribution tag is the canonical use; rotating
the key rotates every pseudonym). The result is deliberately PUBLIC despite the private key: an HMAC
tag reveals nothing about the key by construction — irreversibility IS the sound declassification —
so this is the one prim whose result the runtime does not taint private. Deterministic, so a replay
recomputes the same tag.
declarations.name: hmac_sha256

parameters.documentation: The secret key material; the tag is stable per key and unforgeable without it.
parameters.label: key

parameters.documentation: The text to tag, as its UTF-8 bytes; public, like `sha256`'s.
parameters.label: text

key.description: The secret key material; the tag is stable per key and unforgeable without it.

text.description: The text to tag, as its UTF-8 bytes; public, like `sha256`'s.

declarations.signature: primitive agent hmac_sha256(key: string of private, text: string) -> string

The `file` a handle names is gone — it was `free`d, or the id never named a blob in this project (a
model hallucinating a `$katari_ref`). One error covers both: a slim handle cannot tell which, and a program

declarations.name: gone
declarations.signature: data gone(message: string)

`from_base64` — catch it to fall back when a model or upstream API hands back a corrupt base64 payload.
declarations.name: malformed_base64
declarations.signature: data malformed_base64(message: string)

declarations.documentation:
The file's bytes, base64-encoded — the inline shape multimodal model APIs take. The whole content
materialises as one string, so mind the size (a large file makes a large request body). Throws `gone` if the
handle no longer names a live blob (`free`d, or a made-up id).
declarations.name: read_base64
declarations.signature: primitive agent read_base64(value: file) -> string with prelude.throw[gone]

The file's recorded MIME type (e.g. "image/png"), read from the project's file catalog; "" when
none was recorded. Throws `gone` if the handle no longer names a live blob.
declarations.name: content_type
declarations.signature: primitive agent content_type(value: file) -> string with prelude.throw[gone]

handle no longer names a live blob.
declarations.name: size
declarations.signature: primitive agent size(value: file) -> integer with prelude.throw[gone]

declarations.documentation:
Make a `file` from a base64 string — the engine's blob producer, for lifting a model's / API's embedded
base64 (a gemini `inline_data` image) OFF the value plane and INTO a real blob handle, so the heavy bytes
travel runtime-side like any other file. The new file is owned by the current run and reclaimed with it (or
explicitly, via `free`). Two calls with the SAME bytes are DIFFERENT files (a file is a resource, not a
literal). Throws `malformed_base64` if @content@ is not valid base64.
declarations.name: from_base64

parameters.documentation: The file's bytes, base64-encoded.
parameters.label: content

parameters.documentation: The MIME type to record (e.g. "image/png"); "" to record none.
parameters.label: content_type

content_type.description: The MIME type to record (e.g. "image/png"); "" to record none.

declarations.signature: primitive agent from_base64(content: string, content_type: string) -> file with prelude.throw[malformed_base64]

declarations.documentation:
Release a file the current run owns, freeing its bytes now rather than at run teardown — for a large,
short-lived intermediate (a decoded image already handed to a model). Idempotent and silent: freeing an
already-gone file, or one the run does NOT own (a user-uploaded file, whose lifetime is the file API's), is a

a freed handle throws `gone`.
declarations.name: free
declarations.signature: primitive agent free(value: file) -> null

declarations.name: fetch_error

declarations.documentation:
Perform an HTTP request to @url@ with @method@ (e.g. "GET" / "POST"), the given @headers@ and @body@.
The @body@ is one of `http.text` / `http.binary` / `http.multipart` / `http.json` (a `file` in any of them
is read from the blob store at the send boundary, never materialised earlier). Each header value AND a
private body surface (a `text`'s content, a `json`'s tree) may be a secret, submitted to @url@'s server,
while @url@ and @method@ stay public. Returns the response @status@ code, its @headers@ (names lowercased;
repeated headers joined with ", ") and its @body@ text. A request that never completes throws `fetch_error`
(catchable with `use handler { request throw(error: http.fetch_error) -> never { ... } }`).
declarations.name: fetch

parameters.label: headers

declarations.documentation:
Perform an HTTP request to @url@ with @method@, the given @headers@ and @body@ — EXACTLY `fetch`'s
request — but capture the RESPONSE body as a downloaded `file` rather than as text. The bytes land in the
blob store and the reply carries only the slim @file@ HANDLE; the raw bytes (and their base64) never touch
the value plane, the durable call record, or the trace. This is the receive-side twin of a `binary`
REQUEST body, and it exists for the same reason: to keep a payload's bytes OFF the value plane. A plain
`fetch` of a megabyte image would read it into the response `body` STRING, dragging that text (and its
base64, once re-encoded) through every value, event, and trace it flows into — whereas `fetch_file` streams
it straight to a blob and hands back a handle. Reach for it to download a file by URL: an image, a PDF, a
CSV export, a release artifact. It is NOT for a base64 field buried inside a JSON reply (a data-URI in an
API's JSON document) — `fetch_file` only ever captures the WHOLE response body; decode an embedded base64
string with `files.from_base64` after an ordinary `fetch`. The downloaded @file@'s recorded content type is
the response's `Content-Type` (falling back to `application/octet-stream` when the server sent none).
Returns the response @status@ code (branch on it exactly like `fetch` — a non-2xx reply's body is still
captured to a @file@, so a caller inspects @status@ before trusting the download), its @headers@ (names
lowercased; repeated headers joined with ", "), and the downloaded @file@. A request that never completes
throws `fetch_error`, exactly like `fetch`.
declarations.name: fetch_file

parameters.documentation: The HTTP method, e.g. "GET" / "POST" (case-insensitive). For GET / HEAD the @body@ is not sent.
parameters.label: method

parameters.documentation: Request headers by name; each value may be a secret, revealed only to @url@'s server.
parameters.label: headers

parameters.documentation: The request body: `http.text` / `http.binary` / `http.multipart` / `http.json`; dropped for GET / HEAD.
parameters.label: body

body.description: The request body: `http.text` / `http.binary` / `http.multipart` / `http.json`; dropped for GET / HEAD.

headers.description: Request headers by name; each value may be a secret, revealed only to @url@'s server.

method.description: The HTTP method, e.g. "GET" / "POST" (case-insensitive). For GET / HEAD the @body@ is not sent.

url.description: The absolute URL to request; public by type (a URL leaks into logs and proxies, so a secret here is a type error).

reply PARSED into its document value. This is the canonical one-call shape of a JSON API integration: build
the body as an ordinary record / array / scalar tree, post it, and read the reply as a value — no manual
`json.stringify` / `json.parse` around the call. @body@ AND each header value may be a secret (an auth token
— an "Authorization" of "Bearer <key>" for OpenAI, an "x-goog-api-key" for Gemini — or a `refresh_token`
in the body of an OAuth exchange): both are submitted only to @url@'s server, which stays public. A `file`
placed anywhere in @body@ rides as base64 (the `http.json` slot contract). The Content-Type defaults to
application/json unless a header overrides it. A non-2xx status throws `status_error` (its body text
attached); a transport failure throws `fetch_error`; a 2xx body that is not JSON throws `json.parse_error`
(a JSON API that broke its promise) — an empty 2xx body is `null`. To send already-serialized text, or to
keep the raw reply text, call `fetch` directly.

discharges it from its own, so a tool tagged `scope` cannot outlive the `provide` that introduced it. A
generated `katari mcp pull` binding declares its own module-local marker instead; distinct nullary markers
never merge and never widen, so there is no covariance to reason about.

declarations.documentation:
Plug an MCP server's tools into a program for the extent of @continuation@, as a scoped provider —
the `use mcp.provide(url = ..., auth = ...)` form. The runtime lists the server (a missing or dead
`oauth` credential pauses on an authorization escalation and retries once answered; rejected `headers`
material throws `auth_error`; a rejected listing throws `server_error`), hands @continuation@
a `toolbox[Scope]` of one runtime-minted agent per tool (each carrying the server signature — for
`reflection.get_metadata` and call-site validation — and the descriptor it was listed with), and settles
with the continuation's result. `Scope` rides the continuation's row (that is what a tool call raises) and
is DISCHARGED from `provide`'s own row, so a tool cannot escape the block: the scope closes when
@continuation@ returns (or the run is cancelled), and a stray later call is rejected as a typed
`server_error`. `Scope` is the marker the tools are gated by — the built-in `mcp.scope` for the dynamic
path, or a generated binding's module-local marker; pass it explicitly as the first `[...]` argument
(`mcp.provide[mcp.scope](...)`), and the toolbox binder's annotation must agree. Discharging `Scope` is
`provide`'s alone (only it opens the connection), so a live tool context cannot be forged. @url@ is a plain
routing value: the runtime connects and caches under the `{url, auth}` descriptor.
DECLARE ONE MARKER PER LOGICAL CONNECTION. When you call `provide` directly you choose `Scope` yourself:
share ONE marker across two connections and their scopes MERGE at the type level (the two servers' tools
become mutually substitutable in a row that carries the marker) — the same widening the old dynamic-URL
`toolbox[string]` had, no worse. It is only a TYPE distinction: routing and the live-`provide` backstop are
always enforced by each tool value's own `{url, auth}` descriptor, so a call never reaches the wrong
server — at worst a tool whose `provide` has closed fails with a typed `server_error`. A `katari mcp pull`
binding needs no such discipline: its module namespace mints a distinct marker (`github.connection`) per
connection automatically, so pulled servers never share a scope. When the toolbox itself is never read —
a pulled binding's tools call through the static `mcp.call` — `open` is the listing-free form of this
same contract.
declarations.name: provide

declarations.documentation:
Open an MCP server connection for the extent of @continuation@ WITHOUT listing the server — the
listing-free form of `provide`, same scoped contract, no toolbox. The runtime registers the
connection's `Scope` (minted for @continuation@'s row, DISCHARGED from `open`'s own — exactly
`provide`'s rule, so a live tool context still cannot be forged) and starts @continuation@
immediately with `null`: no server round-trip happens at open, and the connection tears down when
@continuation@ settles (or the run is cancelled). Tools are reached STATICALLY through
`mcp.call[Scope, T]` under the same `{url, auth}` descriptor — the shape a `katari mcp pull` binding
generates — so prefer `open` wherever the toolbox would be ignored: a pulled binding's `connect`,
and per-call connections, where `provide`'s per-open listing is pure overhead. `provide` remains the
dynamic-toolbox form (list the server, hand runtime-minted tools to an AI loop). Because nothing is
contacted at open, auth surfaces at the FIRST `mcp.call`: a missing or dead `oauth` credential
pauses that call on an authorization escalation, and rejected `headers` material / server failures
are its typed throws.

Open a whole SET of MCP connections under ONE scope for the extent of @continuation@ — the
data-driven form of `provide`. The marker is minted once, UNCONDITIONALLY, whatever the array holds:
an optional connection is an `if` in the DATA (append it to the array or not), never a branch around
the `use`, so conditional connections stop forking the program's shape (the 2×2 explosion). The
continuation receives one toolbox per connection, in input order — flatten what you hand an AI loop
(`array.map` + `record.values` + `array.flatten`). Connections open one by one in order and tear
down in reverse; any connection's listing failure is the same typed error a lone `provide` raises,
and tears the already-open ones down. An empty array runs @continuation@ with no toolboxes — the
same row shape, so callers never branch on emptiness. This must be an external, not a composition:
only the runtime actually opening the scope can discharge the marker (a plain agent composing
`provide`s could not type the empty set — there would be nothing to discharge a never-minted
marker).

declarations.documentation:
Call one tool on an MCP server directly — the static counterpart of `provide`, with no listing and no
minted agent value. The seam the binding modules `katari mcp pull` generates are built on: @tool@ is the
server-declared tool name, @arguments@ its arguments object as a plain value tree (records / arrays /
scalars, and a `file` becomes base64 in place — the same slot contract as `http.json`). The result is
read as a value and checked against @T@ inside the runtime: a `$katari_ref` handle object becomes a REAL
`file` value, records / arrays / scalars land as themselves, a plain-text reply reads only into a
string-shaped @T@, and a mismatch throws `validation_error`. Instantiate @T@ with `unknown` to keep the
reply as a raw document value (the codegen's choice when no `outputSchema` maps); a `$katari_ref` in it
is still a real `file` — the wire-to-value conversion is unconditional, never schema-directed. @T@
appears only in the result, so it is never inferable — instantiate it explicitly; the @Scope@ marker is a
phantom the row never infers, so a caller writes both to `[...]`, `mcp.call[Scope, T](url = ..., ...)` — a
generated binding passes its own module-local marker. Nothing validates @arguments@ before the server does
(unlike a minted tool) — a rejected call throws `server_error`. Scope-gated the same way as a minted tool
(`Scope` on its row): a generated binding calls this only inside a `provide` scope over the same marker and
descriptor, and the runtime rejects a call with no live scope for that descriptor as a typed `server_error`.
declarations.name: call

declarations.documentation:
Publish @tools@ as a live MCP server for the extent of @subscriber@. The runtime mints a fresh,
unguessable capability URL and serves the record's agents as MCP tools there — each record key is
the published tool name, each agent's declared signature the tool's advertised schema. The URL is
the key: possession grants access, nobody without it can call in. @subscriber@ receives the URL,
hands it to whoever should connect (an AI session, a teammate's MCP client), and stays alive while
calls should be served; when it returns the URL deactivates and its result becomes `serve`'s
result. Cancelling the run cancels @subscriber@ and deactivates the URL the same way. The
subscriber's effects flow to the caller's handlers unchanged; the served agents are self-contained
(their effects are handled, or are at most `io` and this module's throws), so any agent fits once its
own effects are handled. A served tool that throws or panics with no handler of its own cancels the
whole endpoint (its failure proxies up and fails the run unless caught above @subscriber@) — wrap a
tool's body in a handler for per-request resilience.
declarations.name: serve

browser flow, or a proactive login) — it does not fail. A transient resolution failure throws

declarations.documentation: Open a nursery for the extent of @continuation@, as a scoped provider — the `use region.provide[region.scope, E](...)` form. It hands @continuation@ a `nursery[Scope, E]` handle whose fibers may raise at most the effects `E`, and settles with the continuation's result. `Scope` rides the continuation's row (that is what a `fork` / `cancel` / `watch` raises) and is DISCHARGED from `provide`'s own row, so no fiber outlives the block: the nursery closes when @continuation@ returns (its still-running fibers are cancelled). Pin `Scope` and the ceiling `E` as the first two type arguments (`region.provide[region.scope, my_effects]`); `R` and the residual outer row are inferred from the continuation. Discharging `Scope` is `provide`'s alone (only it opens the nursery), so a live nursery context cannot be forged. NEST UNDER DISTINCT MARKERS: share one marker across two nurseries and their scopes MERGE (fibers become mutually cancellable), so declare a module-local `effect` per nursery when nesting.
declarations.name: provide

declarations.documentation: Spawn @task@ (applied to @argument@) as a fiber in the nursery @nursery@, returning immediately with a `fiber[Scope]` handle (identity only — for `cancel`; read its runtime-minted id with `fiber_id`). @name@ is an optional opaque tag the runtime echoes back wherever it talks about this fiber (`roster`, `crashed`) — give one to any fiber something might later need to name. @task@ is `-> null`: A FIBER CARRIES NO RESULT. Everything a fiber produces leaves through its ESCALATIONS (surfacing at `watch`) — a task with something to deliver performs a request carrying it as its LAST act, and what the task returns is discarded when it settles. The type makes the discipline total: a `-> T` task does not fit, so a result cannot be silently dropped — it must have been delivered (or deliberately not produced) before the task can end. (`-> never` bodies — a watcher that runs until cancelled — fit by subtyping.) @task@'s effect must fit under the ceiling `E` (a child that raises less is fine; one that raises more is a type error), so every fiber is bounded by `E` — which is exactly what makes `watch` a total obligation. The fiber's escalations do not surface here; they well up at `watch`. Scope-gated (`with Scope`): callable only inside the `provide` that opened this nursery.

declarations.documentation: The nursery's WHITE HOLE: re-emit the fibers' escalations into the enclosing program as the ceiling effect `E`, plus the runtime's own `crashed` event. It returns `never` — it only ever raises, never yields — so install a `handler` (or any row that covers `E | crashed`) around it to service the fibers' requests. Because every fiber's effect fits under `E` and `watch` re-emits the FULL `E`, covering `E | crashed` here covers everything any fiber can surface. This is the ONE channel out of a fiber: a normal completion is silent (the settled `null` is discarded — a task that has something to say says it as its last act), a `cancel` is silent (the canceller knows), and a PANIC — the ending a task cannot report itself — arrives as the typed `crashed` event: the runtime tears the dead fiber down and reports the ending as data, so what a crash MEANS is your handler's decision, not an unwinding accident. Scope-gated (`with Scope`): callable only inside the opening `provide`.

re-emitted (and answered) CONCURRENTLY — one `watch` relays strictly one escalation at a time,
answer awaited, so a single watch serializes the fibers' requests end-to-end no matter how parallel
the fibers or the receiving handler are. The parallelism this opens is only realised by a receiving
`parallel handler`; a sequential (stateful) handler re-serializes at its own FIFO, which is exactly
right when order is the point (a chat loop should keep ONE watch: with several, two messages' turns
can interleave). Plain composition — `parallel for` over `watch` — priced as such; the parallel
scaffolding is why `io` joins the row that a bare `watch` does not carry.

part of the region's total obligation. Not meant to be performed by programs (the runtime is its

declarations.documentation:
The replay signal — the ONE request a `replay` provider catches, and the ONLY performable request this
module exports. A converter performs it to ask that the enclosing block be re-run, carrying the failure it
chose to represent as @failure@ (of the converter's own type @F@). `-> never`: performing it transfers
control to the provider (which applies its delay policy and re-runs) and does not return. This is the whole
seam between policy and mechanism — a provider reasons only about `interrupted`, never about `throw` or
`panic`.
declarations.name: interrupted

parameters.label: failure

declarations.documentation:
Run the continuation once and reify which happened: `ran` with its value, or `signalled` with the failure
it performed `interrupted` on. This is the single boundary where `interrupted` is caught and turned into a
value the loop can `match` on in ordinary control flow (the mechanism-side analog of the old `attempt`, but
catching only the replay signal — never `throw` / `panic`, which the converter already handled).
`interrupted[F]` sits in the continuation's OVERWRITE row because this handler DISCHARGES it (the discord-
provider shape); @F@ is inferred from the continuation and preserved into `signalled`.

declarations.documentation:
Replay the rest of the block on every `interrupted`, unbounded and with NO artificial delay: it re-runs at
once. The retry cadence is therefore set entirely by whatever the converter does BEFORE it signals — e.g. a
converter that performs a human-in-the-loop escalation and parks before signalling gives the attended /
re-auth loop, human-paced with no polling. Never re-raises and never returns on its own; a converter that
rethrows instead of signalling is how a failure leaves this loop. Written `use replay.immediate()`.

parameters.label: continuation

Replay the rest of the block on every `interrupted`, unbounded, with exponential backoff capped at
@max_delay_milliseconds@. For daemons that must stay up across transient failures (e.g. keeping a
`time.watch` alive): it never re-raises and never returns on its own. The backoff delay lives in the loop's
own @delay@ var and grows by @factor@ per replay up to the cap (`math.min`), so the durable state stays flat
across any number of replays. Written
`use replay.forever(initial_delay_milliseconds = ..., factor = ..., max_delay_milliseconds = ...)`.

parameters.label: factor

parameters.label: max_delay_milliseconds

declarations.documentation:
Replay the rest of the block on `interrupted` with exponential backoff, up to @max_attempts@ times. On
failure number n (1-based) with n < @max_attempts@: durably sleep @initial_delay_milliseconds@ *
@factor@^(n-1), then re-run. When the budget is spent (the @max_attempts@-th `interrupted`): re-raise that
failure as a TYPED `throw[F]` — @F@ is the converter's chosen failure representation, so exhaustion keeps the
error typed end to end and never needs to re-panic. The attempt count and delay live in the loop's own vars
(one owner). The exhausted-vs-continue decision is genuine sum dispatch: the ONE comparison of the count to
the budget mints a `replay_after | give_up`, and the `signalled` arm `match`es it once — no code re-tests the
counter. Written `use replay.exponential(initial_delay_milliseconds = ..., factor = ..., max_attempts = ...)`.

declarations.documentation:
A cron schedule: the occurrences of the standard cron @expression@ (the 5-field form, or the 6-field
form whose leading field is seconds) read in the IANA @timezone@ (e.g. "Asia/Tokyo", "UTC"). The
timezone is required and explicit — there is no ambient default, because "every day at 09:00" means a
different instant in each zone and the runtime must not guess which one.
declarations.name: cron

parameters.documentation: 5 fields, or 6 with a leading seconds field; a malformed expression panics the watch.
parameters.label: expression

parameters.documentation: An IANA zone name; an unknown zone panics the watch.
parameters.label: timezone

expression.description: 5 fields, or 6 with a leading seconds field; a malformed expression panics the watch.

timezone.description: An IANA zone name; an unknown zone panics the watch.

declarations.signature: data cron(expression: string, timezone: string)

declarations.name: schedule
declarations.signature: type schedule = interval | cron

declarations.documentation:
Call @deliver_to@ once per @schedule@ occurrence, forever, passing the occurrence's scheduled epoch
millisecond as @time@. `watch` never resolves on its own (`-> never`); it runs until the run is
cancelled, at which point the in-flight delivery is cancelled and the watch tears down. @deliver_to@'s
effects @E@ flow to the caller's handlers unchanged.

Durability. The next occurrence is persisted; a restart re-arms it. If one or more occurrences were
missed while the runtime was down, `watch` fires EXACTLY ONCE immediately on recovery (the earliest
missed occurrence's scheduled time — it does not backfill every missed one), then continues on schedule.
Deliveries are serialized: the next occurrence is not armed until the current delivery settles, so a
@deliver_to@ slower than the interval simply rate-limits the ticks rather than queueing them.

No built-in retry. A @deliver_to@ that throws or panics is NOT retried — the failure propagates and kills
the watch, exactly as an uncaught failure in any callee does. Resilience is composed at the call site (a
`replay` provider plus a converter around @deliver_to@), never baked into `watch`.
declarations.name: watch

parameters.documentation: When occurrences fire: an `interval(...)` or a `cron(...)` value.
parameters.label: schedule

parameters.documentation: Called once per occurrence; its @time@ is the occurrence's scheduled epoch millisecond, not the delivery instant.
parameters.label: deliver_to

declarations.signature: external agent watch[effect E](schedule: schedule, deliver_to: agent(time: number) -> null with E) -> never with E | io from "time"

declarations.documentation: The task settled first: its value.
declarations.name: completed

parameters.documentation: The task's result.
parameters.label: value

declarations.signature: data completed[T](value: T)

declarations.documentation: The deadline passed first; the task's arm was cancelled.
declarations.name: deadline_passed
declarations.signature: data deadline_passed()

declarations.name: raced
declarations.signature: type raced[T] = completed[T] | deadline_passed

declarations.documentation:
`with_deadline`'s settle channel — performed by whichever arm finishes first, handled (and `break`ed
on) inside `with_deadline` alone. Its `lacks` constraint is what reserves it: a task cannot perform it,
so the handler peel stays sound over the task's still-generic row.
declarations.name: race_settled

parameters.documentation: The settling side's outcome.
parameters.label: outcome

declarations.signature: request race_settled[T](outcome: T) -> null

declarations.documentation:
Race @task@ against a @milliseconds@ deadline and return whichever settled first: `completed` with
the task's value, or `deadline_passed` — the loser's arm is cancelled (the ordinary cancel cascade; an
in-flight external call is interrupted at-most-once, like any cancel). The task's own throws are NOT
caught here — they escalate as usual; catch them (`prelude.catch`, or a handler) around or inside the
task as the app prefers.
declarations.name: with_deadline

parameters.documentation: The budget, in milliseconds.
parameters.label: milliseconds

parameters.documentation: The task to race; its row may be anything that does not perform `race_settled`.
parameters.label: task

declarations.signature: agent with_deadline[T, effect E](milliseconds: number, task: agent(value: null) -> T with E) -> raced[T] with E | io

declarations.documentation:
A wall-clock date-time split into its calendar fields (proleptic Gregorian). Produced by `to_civil`
and folded back by `from_civil`; a plain value carrying NO zone of its own — it means whatever offset
you read it at.
declarations.name: civil

parameters.documentation: The calendar year.
parameters.label: year

parameters.documentation: 1 (January) to 12 (December).
parameters.label: month

parameters.documentation: 1 to the month's length (`days_in_month`).
parameters.label: day

declarations.signature: data civil(year: integer, month: integer, day: integer, hour: integer, minute: integer, second: integer, millisecond: integer)

declarations.documentation:
Split an epoch-millisecond instant into its wall-clock fields at a fixed offset (@offset_minutes@
east of UTC; the default 0 reads UTC). `from_civil` at the same offset is the exact inverse.
Sub-millisecond precision is dropped.
declarations.name: to_civil
declarations.signature: agent to_civil(epoch_milliseconds: number, offset_minutes: integer ?= 0) -> civil

declarations.documentation:
Fold wall-clock fields back to an epoch-millisecond instant, reading them at a fixed offset
(@offset_minutes@ east of UTC; the default 0 means the fields are UTC). The exact inverse of
`to_civil` at the same offset. Out-of-range fields FOLD ARITHMETICALLY rather than erroring — month 13
is January of the next year, day 0 is the last day of the previous month, hour 24 is midnight of the
next day — so date arithmetic is plain field arithmetic: `day = value.day + 7` is one week later with
every carry handled.
declarations.name: from_civil
declarations.signature: agent from_civil(value: civil, offset_minutes: integer ?= 0) -> number

declarations.documentation:
The ISO 8601 day of the week — 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday) — of the instant's wall-clock date at
@offset_minutes@ (default UTC).
declarations.name: day_of_week
declarations.signature: agent day_of_week(epoch_milliseconds: number, offset_minutes: integer ?= 0) -> integer

declarations.documentation: Whether @year@ is a Gregorian leap year (divisible by 4, except centuries not divisible by 400).
declarations.name: is_leap_year
declarations.signature: agent is_leap_year(year: integer) -> boolean

declarations.documentation:
The number of days in @month@ (1..12) of @year@ — 28..31, leap-rule aware. A month outside 1..12
first folds into its year like `from_civil` (month 13 is January of the next year).
declarations.name: days_in_month
declarations.signature: agent days_in_month(year: integer, month: integer) -> integer

declarations.documentation:
Format an instant as RFC3339 with millisecond precision — `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmmZ` at the default
UTC offset, the same wall clock with a `±HH:MM` suffix at a non-zero @offset_minutes@. The wire inverse
of `from_rfc3339`. A year outside 0..9999 renders faithfully (every digit, a leading `-`) even though
strict RFC3339 wants exactly four.
declarations.name: to_rfc3339
declarations.signature: agent to_rfc3339(epoch_milliseconds: number, offset_minutes: integer ?= 0) -> string

declarations.documentation:
Parse an RFC3339 timestamp — `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fraction]` followed by `Z` or `±HH:MM` — to an
epoch-millisecond UTC instant, or `null` when the string is not one (like `string.to_integer`).
Validated, not clamped: a month or day that does not exist (February 30th) is `null`, not a silently
carried date. `T` / `Z` also read lowercase; a fraction beyond milliseconds is truncated; a leap
second (`:60`) folds into the next minute.
declarations.name: from_rfc3339
declarations.signature: agent from_rfc3339(value: string) -> number | null

declarations.documentation:
Serve a fresh, dynamically generated public webhook URL for the extent of @subscriber@. The
runtime converts every POST to the URL into a call of @callback@ (JSON body in, JSON result out,
validated against @callback@'s input schema). @subscriber@ receives the URL, registers it wherever
deliveries should come from, and stays alive while they flow; when it returns, the URL is
deactivated and its result becomes `inbound`'s result. Both callables' effects flow to the caller's
handlers unchanged.
declarations.name: inbound

parameters.documentation: Called once per POST. A body failing its input schema is rejected 400 before it runs; its unhandled failure cancels the endpoint.
parameters.label: callback

parameters.documentation: The URL's owner: receives the minted public URL, and the endpoint serves exactly while it runs.
parameters.label: subscriber

declarations.signature: external agent inbound[R, effect E](callback: agent never -> unknown with E, subscriber: agent(url: string) -> R with E) -> R with E from "webhook"
